ety.text: Derived from Classical Persian نُمَای (numāy), the present stem of نَمُودَن (namūdan, “to show, exhibit”), which is also the source of नमूदार (namūdār, “visible”), नुमाइंदा (numāindā, “representative”), नुमाइश (numāiś, “exhibition”).
Borrowed from Sanskrit गलनांक (galanāṃka). By surface analysis, गलन (galan) + अंक (aṅk).

s.g: shriek, scream, roar; trumpet (of an elephant)
x: हाथी चंद्रमा की किरणों की ओर सूंड़ें हिला-हिलाकर अपनी चिंघाड़ों के स्वरों में क्या कह रहे थे?
युद्ध के मैदान में लाशों के ढेर लग गए। खून की नदियाँ बह चलीं। चारों ओर घोड़ों की हिनहिनाहट, हाथियों की चिंघाड़ें, तलवारों की टकराहट, बारूद के फटते गोलों और घायलों की चीख-पुकारों से आसमान गूँजने लगा।

ety.text: Probably of onomatopoeic origin similar to that of Sanskrit चीत्कार (cītkāra, “cries, noise”). Cognate with Punjabi ਚਿੰਘਾਰ /چنگھار (ciṅghār), Romani ćingardel (“to scream, to yell”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Sanskrit युगल (yugala, “pair”). Doublet of युगल (yugal).

s.g: Troy (an ancient city in far northwestern Asia Minor, in modern Turkey)

ety.text: Borrowed from Classical Persian دكاندار (dukān-dār). By surface analysis, दुकान (dukān) + -दार (-dār).

The first element is from Sanskrit दु॒ग्ध (dugdhá, “milk”). The second element has been interpreted as -आरा (-ārā, agentive suffix). McGregor, however, connects the word to Sanskrit *दुग्धहार (*dugdhahāra, literally “milk-carrying”), from दुग्ध (dugdha, “milk”) + हार (hāra, “bearing, carrying”). Compare Gujarati દુધારો (dudhāro, “milkman”).

Hindi verb set पकड़ना (pakaṛnā) पकड़ाना (pakṛānā) पकड़वाना (pakaṛvānā) Inherited from Old Hindi पकडि (pakaḍi), पाकडि (pākaḍi), from Proto-New Indo-Aryan *पक्कडइ (pakkaḍaï), perhaps further from Prakrit पग्ग- (pagga-, “seizes”) + Middle Indo-Aryan -𑀟- (-ḍa-). Cognate to Gujarati પકડવું (pakaḍvũ), Marathi पकडणे (pakaḍṇe).
Borrowed from Sanskrit पलाण्डु (palāṇḍu). Cognate with Assamese পনৰু (ponoru).

ety.text: From भू (bhū, “land”) + संपदा (sampadā, “wealth, estate”). Calque of English real estate.

Borrowed from Classical Persian مُغُل (muġul), ultimately from Middle Mongol ᠮᠣᠩᠭᠤᠯ (mongɣul). Noun sense 2 is a semantic loan from English mogul. Cognate with Bengali মুঘল (mughol), Gujarati મુઘલ (mughal).

s.g: a Mughal, Moghul (a head of the South Asian Mughal dynasty; a member of this dynasty)

Borrowed from Sanskrit षट्कोण (ṣaṭkoṇa). By surface analysis, bahuvrīhi compound of षट् (ṣaṭ, “six”) + कोण (koṇ, “angle, corner”).
